title: Alone, not lonely
hook: being alone isn't loneliness; learn to be at ease by yourself (Discourses 3.13)

segments.voice: Yesterday: train in private, and your line, privately. Did you keep one piece of training entirely to yourself? Day four hundred twenty-one.

A party of two hundred people can be lonelier than a quiet walk by yourself. Some people who live alone are deeply at ease, while some who are never alone feel stranded. A full calendar doesn't promise company, and an empty room doesn't promise loneliness. Being by yourself and feeling forlorn turn out to be two different things. Epictetus heard people in crowded Rome say they'd been left all alone. Today: alone, not lonely.
screen: `LONELY AT A PARTY OF TWO HUNDRED.` → `AT EASE ON A QUIET WALK.` → `FORLORN IN A GREAT CITY.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter thirteen: what solitude is. Epictetus starts by separating two things we usually blur together. Being alone, he says, doesn't make someone forlorn, any more than being in a crowd makes them not forlorn. When we lose a brother, a child or a friend, we say we've been left all alone, even while we're living in Rome, with crowds in the street and neighbors on every side. So what is the forlorn feeling, really? Epictetus says it's being without help, exposed, at the mercy of whatever comes. Then he reaches for an image from Stoic belief about the cosmos. In the Stoic picture he's drawing on, the world goes through cycles, and at the end of each it's drawn back into fire. In that moment, Zeus is alone. Yet he isn't forlorn. He's at rest with himself, thinking about how things are ordered. We should be able to do something like that, Epictetus says: to talk with ourselves, to not need others in order to be at peace, to not be lost when there's no one to fill the hours. He adds a contrast. The emperor, he says, gives the world a great peace: no wars, no pirates, safe roads. But the emperor can't give peace from fever, shipwreck, grief or envy. That inner peace, Epictetus says, has to be learned. And one of its first lessons is learning to sit in an empty room and find that someone you can live with is there.
screen: `ALONE ISN'T THE SAME AS FORLORN.` · `FORLORN MEANS WITHOUT HELP.` · `ZEUS ALONE, AT REST WITH HIMSELF.` · `A PEACE NO EMPEROR CAN GIVE.` · then, large: `ALONE, NOT LONELY.`

segments.voice: Sit somewhere you can be by yourself, even if it's just a corner. Breathe. Notice whether being alone feels restful, or a little uneasy, or both. Don't reach for your phone. Just keep yourself company. Ask, gently, as if talking to a friend: how are you, really? Listen for the answer. Then let the quiet be enough for a while. If you can, give yourself ten minutes like this later today. The bell holds the time.
Alone. Epictetus on solitude: being by yourself isn't the same as being forlorn, and we can learn to be at ease in our own company.
Your line: alone, not lonely. Take ten minutes alone today, no screen, no task, and practice being at ease with yourself. Day four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some people drawn to Stoicism set aside a short time each day to be alone without distractions, treating it as practice in being at ease with themselves.

fork.setup: a student has lost a close friend and says: now I'm all alone, though he lives in crowded Rome. what does Epictetus point out?
options: being alone and being forlorn aren't the same; you can learn to be at ease with yourself.
fork.reveal: he says the forlorn feeling is being without help, and that we can learn to keep ourselves company, the way Zeus is at rest when alone.

original.note: Greek erēmia: solitude, desolation (our word hermit comes from the same root); the subject of Discourses 3.13.

trapdoor: what you thought: lonely people just need more people.
what it means: being forlorn is being without help inside; we can learn to be at ease in our own company.
what a scholar hears: the image of Zeus alone at the world's conflagration (ekpyrōsis) draws on Stoic cosmology, in which the cosmos is periodically resolved into fire.

sources.ref: Discourses 3.13 (what solitude is, and what kind of person a solitary is)

notes: Discourses 3.13 paraphrased: solitude as the condition of a helpless person; being alone vs. being forlorn; losing a brother/son/friend while in Rome amid crowds; Zeus at the conflagration, alone and at rest; conversing with oneself; Caesar's peace (no wars, robbers, pirates) vs. peace from fever, shipwreck, grief, envy. Confirm.
Reviewer edit: Rome softened to 'one of the biggest cities in the world' (whether it was the largest, vs. e.g. Han Luoyang, is debated); screen line changed to 'forlorn in a great city'.
Reviewer edit: 'The Stoics taught' cyclical conflagration softened to 'Many Stoics taught'; some Stoics (e.g. Panaetius, Boethus) doubted ekpyrōsis.
Loneliness can be painful and serious; the script frames being at ease alone as a practice, not as a dismissal of loneliness. Check tone.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook drops the unsourced claim about Rome's size and the superlative 'among the most at ease you'll ever meet'; 'many Stoics taught' became 'the Stoic picture he's drawing on' (3.13 itself uses the conflagration image); howItsDone 'many' softened.
